Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 1) Labour is best defined as:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option2: Regular uterine contractions resulting in progressive cervical dilatation and delivery of the fetus and placenta
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: True labour is characterized by regular uterine contractions that produce progressive cervical effacement and dilatation, culminating in delivery.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 2) The average duration of labour in a primigravida is approximately:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Labour is generally longer in primigravidae, averaging around 12–14 hours.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 3) The average duration of labour in a multiparous woman is approximately:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Multiparous women usually have a shorter labour because of previous cervical and pelvic changes.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 4) The first stage of labour extends from:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option1: Onset of uterine contractions to full cervical dilatation
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option2: Full cervical dilatation to delivery of the fetus
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option3: Delivery of the placenta to 24 hours postpartum
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option4: Delivery of the fetus to delivery of the placenta
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The first stage begins with true labour and ends when the cervix reaches 10 cm dilatation.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 5) The second stage of labour extends from:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option1: Delivery of the fetus to delivery of the placenta
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option2: Onset of labour to full cervical dilatation
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option3: Delivery of the placenta to 2 hours postpartum
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option4: Full cervical dilatation to delivery of the fetus
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The second stage begins after complete cervical dilatation and ends with birth of the baby.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 6) The third stage of labour extends from:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option2: Onset of labour to full dilatation
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option4: Delivery of the fetus to expulsion of the placenta and membranes
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The third stage ends with complete delivery of the placenta and membranes.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 7) The fourth stage of labour refers to:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option1: The first 1–2 hours after placental delivery
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: This is the period of close observation for postpartum hemorrhage and maternal stabilization.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 8) The commonest cause of the onset of labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option2: A complex interaction of maternal, fetal, and placental factors
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Labour results from coordinated endocrine and biochemical changes involving the fetus, placenta, and mother.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 9) The normal frequency of uterine contractions during active labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option3: Three to five contractions every 10 minutes
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Effective labour usually consists of 3–5 contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting 40–60 seconds.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 10) The normal duration of a uterine contraction during active labour is approximately:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Contractions become longer and stronger as labour progresses, typically lasting 40–60 seconds in the active phase.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 11) The most common presentation in normal labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Vertex presentation occurs in about 95% of term singleton pregnancies.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 12) The denominator in a vertex presentation is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: In vertex presentation, fetal position is described according to the occiput.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 13) The most common fetal position in normal labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: LOA is the commonest and most favorable position for vaginal delivery.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 14) The cardinal movements of labour begin with:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Flexion allows the smallest fetal head diameter to present to the birth canal.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 15) The first cardinal movement after engagement is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Following engagement, descent occurs throughout labour and accompanies the other cardinal movements.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 16) The largest transverse diameter of the fetal head is the:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The biparietal diameter measures approximately 9.5 cm and is the largest transverse diameter of the fetal skull.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 17) The engaging diameter of a well-flexed vertex presentation is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: A well-flexed fetal head presents the suboccipitobregmatic diameter (approximately 9.5 cm), facilitating vaginal delivery.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 18) Engagement of the fetal head is said to occur when:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option4: The biparietal diameter passes the pelvic inlet
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Engagement occurs when the widest transverse diameter of the fetal head has passed through the pelvic brim.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 19) Cervical dilatation is complete when it reaches:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Full cervical dilatation (10 cm) marks the end of the first stage of labour.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 20) The gold standard tool for monitoring the progress of labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The partograph is the standard tool for monitoring labour progress and identifying abnormal labour early.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 21) The alert line in a partograph represents cervical dilatation at a rate of:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The alert line represents an expected cervical dilatation rate of 1 cm/hour, helping identify slow progress of labour.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 22) Crossing of the action line on a partograph indicates the need for:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option1: Immediate cesarean section in all cases
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Crossing the action line suggests abnormal labour and requires prompt evaluation and appropriate management.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 23) The most reliable clinical sign of true labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option1: Regular painful contractions with progressive cervical dilatation
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Progressive cervical change differentiates true labour from false labour.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 24) The most common cause of false labour pain is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular, painless or mildly painful contractions without cervical change.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 25) Which of the following is not a feature of true labour?
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: False labour often subsides with rest or sedation, whereas true labour continues.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 26) The most common indication for induction of labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Post-term pregnancy is one of the commonest indications for induction of labour.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 27) Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to induction of labour?
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in major placenta previa; therefore labour should not be induced.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 28) The Bishop score is used to assess:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The Bishop score predicts the likelihood of successful induction of labour.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 29) Which Bishop score indicates a favorable cervix?
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: A Bishop score of 8 or more generally indicates a favorable cervix and a high likelihood of successful induction.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 30) The commonest drug used for cervical ripening is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Misoprostol (PGE₁ analogue) is widely used for cervical ripening and induction of labour.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 31) Oxytocin acts primarily by stimulating:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Oxytocin binds to uterine receptors and stimulates rhythmic uterine contractions.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 32) The most serious complication of oxytocin infusion is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Excessive uterine contractions can lead to fetal distress and uterine rupture.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 33) The most common indication for augmentation of labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Augmentation is performed when labour is established but contractions are inadequate.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 34) Artificial rupture of membranes is also known as:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Amniotomy is the deliberate rupture of fetal membranes to induce or augment labour.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 35) The commonest indication for episiotomy is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option2: To shorten the second stage when indicated
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Routine episiotomy is not recommended; it is performed for specific maternal or fetal indications.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 36) The most commonly performed episiotomy is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Mediolateral episiotomy is preferred because it reduces the risk of extension into the anal sphincter.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 37) The major advantage of mediolateral episiotomy over median episiotomy is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option4: Lower risk of third- and fourth-degree perineal tears
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Mediolateral episiotomy is less likely to extend into the anal sphincter complex.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 38) The commonest indication for cesarean section worldwide is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Previous cesarean delivery is currently the leading indication for cesarean section in many countries.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 39) The most common indication for primary cesarean section is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Among women without a previous cesarean, cephalopelvic disproportion is a common indication for primary cesarean delivery.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 40) The most commonly performed uterine incision in cesarean section is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The lower segment transverse uterine incision is preferred because it is associated with less blood loss, better healing, and a lower risk of uterine rupture in subsequent pregnancies.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 41) The ideal time to perform an episiotomy is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option4: At crowning of the fetal head
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Episiotomy should be performed when the fetal head is crowning and the perineum is thinned out to minimize blood loss and tissue trauma.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 42) The best method for pain relief during normal labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Epidural analgesia provides the most effective pain relief while allowing the mother to remain awake and cooperative.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 43) Which of the following is a contraindication to epidural analgesia?
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Coagulopathy is an absolute contraindication because of the risk of spinal/epidural hematoma.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 44) The most common maternal side effect of epidural analgesia is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Sympathetic blockade causes vasodilation, making hypotension the commonest complication.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 45) Vacuum extraction is contraindicated in:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Vacuum extraction should not be used in face presentation because of the risk of fetal injury.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 46) Forceps delivery requires all of the following except:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Instrumental vaginal delivery should only be attempted after engagement of the fetal head.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 47) The most common indication for vacuum extraction is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Vacuum extraction is commonly used to shorten a prolonged second stage when vaginal delivery is appropriate.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 48) Compared with forceps, vacuum extraction is associated with a higher risk of:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Vacuum extraction has a higher incidence of cephalhematoma and scalp injuries than forceps.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 49) Compared with vacuum extraction, forceps delivery is associated with:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Forceps are more likely to cause maternal soft tissue injury but are less likely to cause scalp injuries than vacuum.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 50) The station of the fetal head is measured in relation to the:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Fetal station is assessed relative to the level of the maternal ischial spines, with 0 station at the spines.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 51) A fetal head at the level of the ischial spines is described as:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Zero station indicates engagement, with the presenting part at the level of the ischial spines.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 52) The first clinical sign of placental separation is usually:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Lengthening of the cord is usually the earliest visible sign of placental separation.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 53) The most reliable sign of placental separation is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option3: Uterus becomes firm, globular, and rises in the abdomen
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: After placental separation, the uterus contracts, becomes firm and globular, and rises in the abdomen—this is the most reliable clinical sign.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 54) Controlled cord traction is performed during:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option4: Active management of the third stage of labour
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Controlled cord traction facilitates placental delivery after signs of placental separation appear.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 55) The single most effective component of active management of the third stage of labour for preventing postpartum hemorrhage is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Administration of oxytocin immediately after birth is the most effective intervention to reduce postpartum hemorrhage.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 56) The uterotonic of choice for routine active management of the third stage of labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Oxytocin (10 IU IM or IV) is the first-line uterotonic because it is highly effective and has fewer adverse effects.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 57) Delayed umbilical cord clamping in a healthy term newborn is generally recommended for at least:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Delayed cord clamping improves neonatal iron stores and reduces the risk of iron deficiency.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 58) The commonest mechanism of placental separation is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Schultze (central) separation is the most common mechanism, with the fetal surface presenting first.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 59) In the Duncan mechanism of placental separation, the placenta separates:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option2: From the lower uterine segment only
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Duncan separation begins at the placental margin, so bleeding is often visible before placental delivery.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 60) A woman in labour develops sudden fetal bradycardia immediately after artificial rupture of membranes. The first diagnosis to exclude is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Sudden fetal bradycardia following amniotomy should immediately raise suspicion for umbilical cord prolapse, an obstetric emergency requiring urgent evaluation.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 61) Which of the following is the most common cause of prolonged first stage of labour?
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Dysfunctional uterine contractions (uterine inertia) are the commonest cause of prolonged first-stage labour.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 62) Failure of the fetal head to descend despite adequate uterine contractions most commonly suggests:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Adequate contractions with no descent strongly suggest mechanical obstruction such as CPD.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 63) The commonest cause of obstructed labour worldwide is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: CPD remains the leading cause of obstructed labour, especially in resource-limited settings.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 64) The most common cause of prolonged second stage of labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option2: Inadequate maternal expulsive efforts or malposition
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Poor maternal pushing, epidural analgesia, or persistent occipitoposterior position commonly prolong the second stage.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 65) Persistent occipitoposterior position most commonly results in:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Persistent occipitoposterior position often causes prolonged labour due to difficult internal rotation.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 66) The cardinal movement immediately following flexion is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Descent accompanies the entire labour process and follows flexion in the sequence of cardinal movements.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 67) The cardinal movement that allows the fetal shoulders to align with the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvis is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Internal rotation positions the shoulders and head to negotiate the maternal pelvis efficiently.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 68) Restitution is defined as:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option1: Realignment of the fetal head with the shoulders after birth of the head
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: After the head is delivered, it rotates to align with the shoulders, which are still inside the pelvis.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 69) External rotation of the fetal head occurs because of:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: As the shoulders rotate internally, the head rotates externally to maintain alignment.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 70) The final cardinal movement of labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Expulsion refers to the delivery of the shoulders and the remainder of the fetal body.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 71) The denominator in breech presentation is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Breech positions are described according to the position of the fetal sacrum.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 72) The denominator in face presentation is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: In face presentation, fetal position is designated by the chin (mentum).

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 73) The denominator in shoulder presentation is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: In transverse lie (shoulder presentation), the acromion process is the denominator.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 74) The fetal skull suture most commonly palpated in a well-flexed vertex presentation is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Vaginal examination commonly identifies the sagittal suture and fontanelles to determine fetal position.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 75) The triangular fontanelle is the:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The posterior fontanelle is small and triangular, helping identify a well-flexed vertex.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 76) The diamond-shaped fontanelle is the:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The anterior fontanelle is diamond-shaped and larger than the posterior fontanelle.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 77) Which pelvic type is most favorable for normal vaginal delivery?
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The gynecoid pelvis has the most favorable dimensions for uncomplicated vaginal delivery.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 78) The fetal head is considered engaged when the biparietal diameter has passed through the:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Engagement occurs once the biparietal diameter has crossed the pelvic brim (inlet).

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 79) Which of the following does not form part of the Bishop score?
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The Bishop score includes cervical dilatation, effacement (or length), consistency, position, and fetal station—not fetal heart rate.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 80) A Bishop score assesses all of the following except:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Estimated fetal weight is not a component of the Bishop score. The score evaluates cervical readiness for induction by assessing dilatation, effacement, consistency, position, and station.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 81) The most common indication for instrumental vaginal delivery is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Instrumental vaginal delivery (forceps or vacuum) is most commonly performed to shorten a prolonged second stage when vaginal delivery is feasible.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 82) A prerequisite for vacuum extraction is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Vacuum extraction requires a fully dilated cervix, ruptured membranes, engaged head, and a known fetal position.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 83) Which of the following is a prerequisite for forceps delivery?
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option3: Engaged fetal head with known position
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Forceps should be applied only when the fetal head is engaged and its position is accurately known.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 84) The most common fetal complication of vacuum extraction is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Vacuum extraction is associated with a higher incidence of scalp injuries and cephalhematoma.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 85) The fetal complication more commonly associated with forceps delivery is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Compression from forceps blades may cause temporary facial nerve palsy.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 86) The best indicator of adequate uterine contractions during labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Effective uterine contractions produce progressive cervical effacement and dilatation.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 87) The most important determinant of successful vaginal delivery is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option2: Pelvic adequacy in relation to fetal size
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Successful vaginal delivery depends primarily on the relationship between the fetal head and maternal pelvis.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 88) Which of the following is not one of the “Three Ps” affecting labour?
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The “Three Ps” of labour are Passenger (fetus), Passage (pelvis), and Powers (uterine contractions).

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 89) The “Passenger” in labour refers to the:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Passenger includes the fetus and its characteristics such as size, presentation, lie, attitude, and position.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 90) The “Powers” of labour consist mainly of:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option1: Uterine contractions and maternal bearing-down efforts
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Primary powers are uterine contractions, while secondary powers are maternal expulsive efforts.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 91) The “Passage” in labour refers to the:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.option1: Birth canal including the bony pelvis and soft tissues
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: The passage comprises the maternal bony pelvis and soft tissues through which the fetus passes.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 92) The most common fetal attitude in normal labour is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: In normal labour, the fetus assumes a flexed attitude, presenting the smallest diameters of the head.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 93) The normal fetal lie at term is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: More than 99% of singleton term pregnancies have a longitudinal lie.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 94) The relationship between the fetal long axis and maternal long axis is known as:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Fetal lie describes the relationship of the fetal axis to the maternal uterine axis.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 95) The relationship of fetal parts to one another is called:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Fetal attitude refers to the degree of flexion or extension of the fetal head and limbs.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 96) The relationship of the denominator to the maternal pelvis is termed:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Position describes the orientation of the fetal denominator (e.g., occiput) in relation to the maternal pelvis.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 97) The fetal part that occupies the lower pole of the uterus is called the:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Presentation refers to the fetal part that first enters the pelvic inlet.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 98) The presenting diameter in a face presentation is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: In a fully extended face presentation, the engaging diameter is the submentobregmatic diameter (≈9.5 cm).

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 99) The presenting diameter in a brow presentation is:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Brow presentation presents the mentovertical diameter (≈13.5 cm), making vaginal delivery usually impossible if persistent.

Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.question: 100) A persistent brow presentation most commonly requires:
Normal Labour & Operative Obstetrics.exp: Persistent brow presentation presents the largest cephalic diameter and usually cannot deliver vaginally, making cesarean section the preferred mode of delivery.
